details.title: AI Literacy for the Modern Workplace (Generative AI Upskill)
details.description: A compact course by Anthony Alicea: how LLMs are trained and run (determinism, inference, context), prompt anatomy and workplace uses with practice, a risk section on hallucinations, privacy, drift, over-reliance, confirmation bias, sycophancy and hidden instructions (prompt injection), and human-AI collaboration with a risk-value decision framework. Includes practice items, assignments and a Udemy role-play exercise; no quizzes.
details.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N3 Partial 62%; N4 Weak 17%; N6 Partial 38%; N14 Weak 10%; R3.1 Weak 17% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.
details.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): Manual practice to prevent skill erosion is explicitly explained; prompt-injection lesson is awareness, not tester training. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit.

audit.note: Manual practice to prevent skill erosion is explicitly explained; prompt-injection lesson is awareness, not tester training.
audit.basis: Public provider/source desk review — syllabus evidence, not course completion
audit.priorFit: Best generic Base option in the batch for N3 (covers hallucination, sycophancy, non-determinism, over-reliance and prompt injection in one 1h45 course); not cyber-specific and nothing on agents.
audit.priorCoverage: N3 Base 62% Partial; N6 Entry 38% Partial; N4 Base 17% Weak

requirementDetails.title: Overview of AI security risks
requirementDetails.description: Recognise the main categories of security risk affecting AI systems and agents, informed by OWASP's LLM and agentic risk frameworks: instruction manipulation, sensitive-information disclosure, unsafe output handling, excessive permissions or actions, compromised components or information sources, and service disruption or uncontrolled resource consumption. Explain a simple example of each and identify an appropriate precaution or escalation route. Foundation awareness does not require threat modelling or memorising framework identifiers.

evidence.title: AI Literacy for the Modern Workplace (Generative AI Upskill)
evidence.evidence: V11 reassessment (18 October 2026). The reviewed syllabus teaches selected attack/risk families or precautions. Coverage of all six families with examples and a precaution/escalation response is not evidenced. No full overview credit is inferred from a framework name or a narrow lab. Reviewed syllabus: A compact course by Anthony Alicea: how LLMs are trained and run (determinism, inference, context), prompt anatomy and workplace uses with practice, a risk section on hallucinations, privacy, drift, over-reliance, confirmation bias, sycophancy and hidden instructions (prompt injection), and human-AI collaboration with a risk-value decision framework. Includes practice items, assignments and a Udemy role-play exercise; no quizzes.

details.description: Arize AI short course with 15 video lessons and 5 code labs. Learners build an agent with a router, skills and memory, add tracing, then add router and skill evaluations, trajectory evaluations (convergence score), and structured experiments that vary prompts, models or logic. details.title: Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026
details.description: A peer-reviewed reference guide to the ten main risks of agentic applications (ASI01-ASI10): goal hijack, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, agentic supply chain, unexpected code execution, memory and context poisoning, insecure inter-agent communication, cascading failures, human-agent trust exploitation, and rogue agents. Each entry has attack scenarios and mitigations. The appendices map the risks to the LLM Top 10, CycloneDX/AIBOM and the Non-Human Identities Top 10, and include an incident tracker. It is reading only.

details.title: Taxonomy of Failure Modes in Agentic AI Systems v2.0
details.description: Microsoft AI Red Team's 16-page update of its agentic failure-mode taxonomy, based on a year of red-team engagements. It adds seven failure modes (agentic supply chain compromise, goal hijacking, inter-agent trust escalation, computer-use visual attacks, session context contamination, MCP/plugin abuse incl. tool description poisoning, capability disclosure) and reports human-in-the-loop bypass via consent fatigue as the most exploited. The mitigations section covers supply-chain controls, zero-trust inter-agent identity, consent architecture hardening (tiered approvals by reversibility, decomposed actions, approval-rate monitoring), session hardening and output filtering, and maps to OWASP, CSA, MITRE and NIST. Reading only; no exercises.

details.title: Agent Control Standard (ACS)
details.description: An early-stage (v0.1.0) open specification for runtime control of AI agents. A separate Guardian receives nineteen lifecycle hooks (for example tool-call request and result, memory read/write) and returns allow, deny, modify, ask or defer. Deterministic policy (OPA/Rego, Cedar) runs first, and there are an audit chain, OpenTelemetry/OCSF tracing and an AgBOM inventory. A reference Guardian with Claude Code and OpenCode shims can be run, but there is no tutorial or exercise; the README notes known gaps (unsigned wire, fail-open default).

details.title: MCP: Model Context Protocol for AI Governance & Security
details.description: No-code course on the Model Context Protocol for governance, security and compliance professionals. It covers roles and session model, primitives (tools, resources, prompts, sampling, roots), the security model (consent, credentials, allowlists, OAuth 2.1/PKCE), prompt injection via tool descriptions, forbidden patterns and server vetting. Later sections compare MCP with A2A and function calling and cover enterprise gateways, registries, auditing MCP traffic, and the EU AI Act, ISO 42001 and NIST AI RMF. Assessment is two practice tests and a role play; there are no hands-on labs.

details.title: AI Agent Security: AI Security
details.description: Eden Marco's hands-on course: learners deploy a vulnerable web-based help-desk agent on Google Cloud, then exploit and fix it: excessive agency and blast radius, broken access control fixed with RBAC on tool calls, data exfiltration via indirect prompt injection (traced in LangSmith) fixed with tool validation and data boundaries, and memory poisoning. A short opening section covers agentic coding security and treating Skills and MCP servers as code execution. No graded quizzes; practice is exploit/fix along with the instructor.
details.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N2 Weak 10%; N3 Weak 24%; N4 Weak 14%; N5 Weak 11%; N7 Weak 13%; N8 Weak 27%; N9 Weak 7%; N12 Partial 44%; R3.1 Partial 50%; R5.1 Weak 11% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.
details.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): Exploit/fix walkthrough uses LangSmith traces and RBAC on tool calls; Skills/MCP are treated as code execution. No full supervisor cycle or general evaluation suite. The prompt-hardening lecture synopsis explicitly explains why non-deterministic models cannot provide a guaranteed security boundary. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit.

audit.note: Exploit/fix walkthrough uses LangSmith traces and RBAC on tool calls; Skills/MCP are treated as code execution. No full supervisor cycle or general evaluation suite. details.title: Agent Control Standard (ACS)
details.description: An early-stage (v0.1.0) open specification for runtime control of AI agents. A separate Guardian receives nineteen lifecycle hooks (for example tool-call request and result, memory read/write) and returns allow, deny, modify, ask or defer. Deterministic policy (OPA/Rego, Cedar) runs first, and there are an audit chain, OpenTelemetry/OCSF tracing and an AgBOM inventory. A reference Guardian with Claude Code and OpenCode shims can be run, but there is no tutorial or exercise; the README notes known gaps (unsigned wire, fail-open default).
details.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N2 Weak 10%; N7 Weak 7%; N12 Weak 30%; N13 Weak 11%; R4.1 Weak 22%; R5.1 Partial 39%; R6.1 Partial 33% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.
details.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): Guardian lifecycle hooks, action audit and AgBOM support partial inventory/control-assurance learning. Early specification and conformance checks are not learner exercises. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit.

audit.note: Guardian lifecycle hooks, action audit and AgBOM support partial inventory/control-assurance learning. Early specification and conformance checks are not learner exercises.

details.title: Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services
details.description: Joint Five Eyes guidance (ASD ACSC, CISA, NSA, Canadian Cyber Centre, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK) that defines agentic AI and its components and sets out five risk categories: privilege, design and configuration, behavioural, structural and accountability. It gives best practices across design, development, deployment and operation, for example distinct cryptographic agent identity, a centralised policy decision point, JIT credentials, logs agents cannot write to, human approval for high-impact or irreversible actions, and graduated autonomy with rollback. An appendix lists prerequisites. It is reading only.

details.title: AI Literacy for the Modern Workplace (Generative AI Upskill)
details.description: A compact course by Anthony Alicea: how LLMs are trained and run (determinism, inference, context), prompt anatomy and workplace uses with practice, a risk section on hallucinations, privacy, drift, over-reliance, confirmation bias, sycophancy and hidden instructions (prompt injection), and human-AI collaboration with a risk-value decision framework. Includes practice items, assignments and a Udemy role-play exercise; no quizzes.
details.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N3 Partial 62%; N4 Weak 17%; N6 Partial 38%; N14 Weak 10%; R3.1 Weak 17% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.

Includes practice items, assignments and a Udemy role-play exercise; no quizzes.

details.description: A peer-reviewed reference guide to the ten main risks of agentic applications (ASI01-ASI10): goal hijack, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, agentic supply chain, unexpected code execution, memory and context poisoning, insecure inter-agent communication, cascading failures, human-agent trust exploitation, and rogue agents. details.title: Taxonomy of Failure Modes in Agentic AI Systems v2.0
details.description: Microsoft AI Red Team's 16-page update of its agentic failure-mode taxonomy, based on a year of red-team engagements. It adds seven failure modes (agentic supply chain compromise, goal hijacking, inter-agent trust escalation, computer-use visual attacks, session context contamination, MCP/plugin abuse incl. tool description poisoning, capability disclosure) and reports human-in-the-loop bypass via consent fatigue as the most exploited. The mitigations section covers supply-chain controls, zero-trust inter-agent identity, consent architecture hardening (tiered approvals by reversibility, decomposed actions, approval-rate monitoring), session hardening and output filtering, and maps to OWASP, CSA, MITRE and NIST. Reading only; no exercises.

details.title: MCP: Model Context Protocol for AI Governance & Security
details.description: No-code course on the Model Context Protocol for governance, security and compliance professionals. It covers roles and session model, primitives (tools, resources, prompts, sampling, roots), the security model (consent, credentials, allowlists, OAuth 2.1/PKCE), prompt injection via tool descriptions, forbidden patterns and server vetting. Later sections compare MCP with A2A and function calling and cover enterprise gateways, registries, auditing MCP traffic, and the EU AI Act, ISO 42001 and NIST AI RMF. Assessment is two practice tests and a role play; there are no hands-on labs.

details.title: Agent Control Standard (ACS)
details.description: An early-stage (v0.1.0) open specification for runtime control of AI agents. A separate Guardian receives nineteen lifecycle hooks (for example tool-call request and result, memory read/write) and returns allow, deny, modify, ask or defer. Deterministic policy (OPA/Rego, Cedar) runs first, and there are an audit chain, OpenTelemetry/OCSF tracing and an AgBOM inventory. A reference Guardian with Claude Code and OpenCode shims can be run, but there is no tutorial or exercise; the README notes known gaps (unsigned wire, fail-open default).

details.title: Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services
details.description: Joint Five Eyes guidance (ASD ACSC, CISA, NSA, Canadian Cyber Centre, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK) that defines agentic AI and its components and sets out five risk categories: privilege, design and configuration, behavioural, structural and accountability. It gives best practices across design, development, deployment and operation, for example distinct cryptographic agent identity, a centralised policy decision point, JIT credentials, logs agents cannot write to, human approval for high-impact or irreversible actions, and graduated autonomy with rollback. An appendix lists prerequisites. It is reading only.

details.title: AI Literacy for the Modern Workplace (Generative AI Upskill)
details.description: A compact course by Anthony Alicea: how LLMs are trained and run (determinism, inference, context), prompt anatomy and workplace uses with practice, a risk section on hallucinations, privacy, drift, over-reliance, confirmation bias, sycophancy and hidden instructions (prompt injection), and human-AI collaboration with a risk-value decision framework. Includes practice items, assignments and a Udemy role-play exercise; no quizzes.
details.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N3 Partial 62%; N4 Weak 17%; N6 Partial 38%; N14 Weak 10%; R3.1 Weak 17% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.
details.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): Manual practice to prevent skill erosion is explicitly explained; prompt-injection lesson is awareness, not tester training. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit.

audit.note: Manual practice to prevent skill erosion is explicitly explained; prompt-injection lesson is awareness, not tester training.

requirementDetails.title: Overview of AI security risks
requirementDetails.description: Recognise the main categories of security risk affecting AI systems and agents, informed by OWASP's LLM and agentic risk frameworks: instruction manipulation, sensitive-information disclosure, unsafe output handling, excessive permissions or actions, compromised components or information sources, and service disruption or uncontrolled resource consumption. Explain a simple example of each and identify an appropriate precaution or escalation route. Foundation awareness does not require threat modelling or memorising framework identifiers.
requirementDetails.gap: Can be completed through another assessed resource

evidence.title: AI Literacy for the Modern Workplace (Generative AI Upskill)
evidence.evidence: V11 reassessment (18 October 2026). The reviewed syllabus teaches selected attack/risk families or precautions. Coverage of all six families with examples and a precaution/escalation response is not evidenced. No full overview credit is inferred from a framework name or a narrow lab. Reviewed syllabus: A compact course by Anthony Alicea: how LLMs are trained and run (determinism, inference, context), prompt anatomy and workplace uses with practice, a risk section on hallucinations, privacy, drift, over-reliance, confirmation bias, sycophancy and hidden instructions (prompt injection), and human-AI collaboration with a risk-value decision framework. Includes practice items, assignments and a Udemy role-play exercise; no quizzes.
evidence.change: V11 reassessment; prior v10 score: not assessed

Best-fit Skills candidate; failure-mode sections, attached eval cases, monthly reviews and owned deprecation rules are not all evidenced, so no full N8 credit. details.title: Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026
details.description: A peer-reviewed reference guide to the ten main risks of agentic applications (ASI01-ASI10): goal hijack, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, agentic supply chain, unexpected code execution, memory and context poisoning, insecure inter-agent communication, cascading failures, human-agent trust exploitation, and rogue agents. Each entry has attack scenarios and mitigations. The appendices map the risks to the LLM Top 10, CycloneDX/AIBOM and the Non-Human Identities Top 10, and include an incident tracker. It is reading only.
details.coverageAtAssessment: Historical pre-v11 snapshot: N2 Weak 10%; N3 Weak 29%; N4 Weak 19%; N5 Weak 17%; N7 Partial 40%; N8 Weak 27%; N12 Partial 44%; N13 Weak 6%; N14 Weak 10%; R1.1 Weak 11%; R3.1 Partial 50%; R4.1 Weak 22%; R5.1 Partial 56%; R9.1 Weak 19% | Current v11 results: Coverage sheet.
details.limitations: V8 (15 Oct 2026): Agentic Top 10 mitigations include approval, trust abuse, bounded identity, supply chain and rogue-agent containment; no exercises or complete incident playbooks. Prior fit note retained in V8 audit.

details.title: Taxonomy of Failure Modes in Agentic AI Systems v2.0
details.description: Microsoft AI Red Team's 16-page update of its agentic failure-mode taxonomy, based on a year of red-team engagements. It adds seven failure modes (agentic supply chain compromise, goal hijacking, inter-agent trust escalation, computer-use visual attacks, session context contamination, MCP/plugin abuse incl. tool description poisoning, capability disclosure) and reports human-in-the-loop bypass via consent fatigue as the most exploited. The mitigations section covers supply-chain controls, zero-trust inter-agent identity, consent architecture hardening (tiered approvals by reversibility, decomposed actions, approval-rate monitoring), session hardening and output filtering, and maps to OWASP, CSA, MITRE and NIST. Reading only; no exercises.

details.title: MCP: Model Context Protocol for AI Governance & Security
details.description: No-code course on the Model Context Protocol for governance, security and compliance professionals. It covers roles and session model, primitives (tools, resources, prompts, sampling, roots), the security model (consent, credentials, allowlists, OAuth 2.1/PKCE), prompt injection via tool descriptions, forbidden patterns and server vetting. Later sections compare MCP with A2A and function calling and cover enterprise gateways, registries, auditing MCP traffic, and the EU AI Act, ISO 42001 and NIST AI RMF. Assessment is two practice tests and a role play; there are no hands-on labs.

details.title: Prepare an enterprise governance strategy for AI agents
details.description: A short beginner Microsoft Learn module (9 units) for leaders and administrators. It covers governance through identity (per-agent Entra Agent ID), containment (OS-level execution containers, workload isolation) and management (policies that allow, block or elevate actions, plus audit). It shows matching controls to agent risk through a three-agent example, a control-plane versus execution-layer model, and an Audit-Define-Refresh strategy (inventory and owners, per-agent identity and sponsor requirements). It ends with a pitch for Windows 11 Pro and Copilot+ PCs and has a knowledge check only.

details.description: Eden Marco's hands-on course: learners deploy a vulnerable web-based help-desk agent on Google Cloud, then exploit and fix it: excessive agency and blast radius, broken access control fixed with RBAC on tool calls, data exfiltration via indirect prompt injection (traced in LangSmith) fixed with tool validation and data boundaries, and memory poisoning. details.title: Agent Control Standard (ACS)
details.description: An early-stage (v0.1.0) open specification for runtime control of AI agents. A separate Guardian receives nineteen lifecycle hooks (for example tool-call request and result, memory read/write) and returns allow, deny, modify, ask or defer. Deterministic policy (OPA/Rego, Cedar) runs first, and there are an audit chain, OpenTelemetry/OCSF tracing and an AgBOM inventory. A reference Guardian with Claude Code and OpenCode shims can be run, but there is no tutorial or exercise; the README notes known gaps (unsigned wire, fail-open default).

evidence.title: AI Ethics & Responsible Use of AI – A Beginner’s Guide
evidence.evidence: V11 reassessment (18 October 2026). Security/privacy risks, safety constraints or controls are named in the retained public syllabus, but a coherent explanation of the revised security-risk overview is not established. Reviewed syllabus: A beginner course narrated by a text-to-speech voice. It walks through four pillars of responsible AI with an example for each, AI bias, four 'Modern Risks' lectures (per the description: hallucinations, misinformation, deepfakes, data leaks), when to use and not use AI, and a S.A.F.E. checklist. There are no quizzes or exercises, only a template and a reading list.

details.description: Arize AI short course with 15 video lessons and 5 code labs. Learners build an agent with a router, skills and memory, add tracing, then add router and skill evaluations, trajectory evaluations (convergence score), and structured experiments that vary prompts, models or logic. details.title: Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026
details.description: A peer-reviewed reference guide to the ten main risks of agentic applications (ASI01-ASI10): goal hijack, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, agentic supply chain, unexpected code execution, memory and context poisoning, insecure inter-agent communication, cascading failures, human-agent trust exploitation, and rogue agents. Each entry has attack scenarios and mitigations. The appendices map the risks to the LLM Top 10, CycloneDX/AIBOM and the Non-Human Identities Top 10, and include an incident tracker. It is reading only.

details.title: Levels of Autonomy for agentic AI (L0–L5)
details.description: Blog post by the CSA CEO proposing six autonomy levels for agentic AI (L0 no autonomy to L5 self-directed), modelled on SAE J3016. For each level it describes the human role, the controls required, who authorises it and how often it is reviewed, and it argues that autonomy boundaries must be enforced technically. details.title: Taxonomy of Failure Modes in Agentic AI Systems v2.0
details.description: Microsoft AI Red Team's 16-page update of its agentic failure-mode taxonomy, based on a year of red-team engagements. It adds seven failure modes (agentic supply chain compromise, goal hijacking, inter-agent trust escalation, computer-use visual attacks, session context contamination, MCP/plugin abuse incl. tool description poisoning, capability disclosure) and reports human-in-the-loop bypass via consent fatigue as the most exploited. The mitigations section covers supply-chain controls, zero-trust inter-agent identity, consent architecture hardening (tiered approvals by reversibility, decomposed actions, approval-rate monitoring), session hardening and output filtering, and maps to OWASP, CSA, MITRE and NIST. Reading only; no exercises.

details.title: Agent Control Standard (ACS)
details.description: An early-stage (v0.1.0) open specification for runtime control of AI agents. A separate Guardian receives nineteen lifecycle hooks (for example tool-call request and result, memory read/write) and returns allow, deny, modify, ask or defer. A reference Guardian with Claude Code and OpenCode shims can be run, but there is no tutorial or exercise; the README notes known gaps (unsigned wire, fail-open default).

details.title: Prepare an enterprise governance strategy for AI agents
details.description: A short beginner Microsoft Learn module (9 units) for leaders and administrators. It covers governance through identity (per-agent Entra Agent ID), containment (OS-level execution containers, workload isolation) and management (policies that allow, block or elevate actions, plus audit). details.title: Agent Control Standard (ACS)
details.description: An early-stage (v0.1.0) open specification for runtime control of AI agents. A separate Guardian receives nineteen lifecycle hooks (for example tool-call request and result, memory read/write) and returns allow, deny, modify, ask or defer. rows.rationale: Solver-selected coverage benchmark under this profile and budget. This selection has not been endorsed for delivery suitability; review prerequisites, framework overlap and task relevance before use.
rows.audience: Assign only where the profile reflects actual work; approved tools and operational permissions are separate decisions.

recommendation.message: Optimal coverage within these constraints; ties resolved by hours, then course count.

rationale.all: Assign the 1h45 AI-literacy course within a 2h Foundation course budget. Social engineering and deepfake impersonation need a brief awareness treatment for cyber staff: use a 10-minute segment within the existing bank session for recognition, independent trusted-channel verification and escalation. Do not assign the full INT-2787 social-engineering course to Foundation. Keep N5.8 risk overview separate from N5.4 bank attack examples. Proposed internal learning remains unassessed.
rationale.entry: Build with Andrew provides accessible, no-code prompting and iteration. Its app project is an L1 practice example; it does not demonstrate agent-builder competence. The bank lab teaches work context, checking and accountable use.
rationale.practitioner: Evaluating AI Agents supplies tracing and evaluation practice; Agent Skills adds reusable instructions and tool use; inherited safe-use knowledge and agent-security guidance support supervision. Internal exercises supply ownership, recovery and domain-specific sign-off. Python readiness is required for the evaluation course; validate Skills exercises in the pilot.
rationale.technical: A coherent multi-agent programme develops build and deployment skills; Reasoning with o1 adds routing and cost/latency decisions; Improving Accuracy adds known-answer evaluation. This pathway is for code-ready builders. Pilot all notebooks, especially o1-era examples, before assigning; the coached adaptation serves no-code builders. Security architecture and infrastructure remain separately assigned roles.
rationale.governance: Governance fundamentals and an autonomy framework support a bank-specific risk case; governance responsibility does not require L3.
rationale.grc-builder: The same governance role content is layered over L3 only for people who also build agents.
rationale.leadership: A short autonomy framework supports decision vocabulary. The bank studio and quarterly forums teach workflow change, accountability and vendor decisions using bank evidence.
rationale.cdc: Inherited agent-security teaching is supplemented by a timed bank incident drill. A separate introductory course would repeat inherited content.
rationale.forensics: Careful Adoption adds protected logging and recovery guidance; a trace-preservation and reconstruction exercise supplies practical evidence.
rationale.threat-intelligence: Agent threat research supports N5.7 threat-landscape responsibility, with bank-specific monitoring and detection updates.
rationale.idp: Assign the governance branch to staff who assess AI/data risk. DLP-only staff should retain relevant supervision outcomes and remove governance responsibilities they do not hold.
rationale.biso: Governance fundamentals and the agent-security matrix support risk review and assurance; the combined branch needs a provisional 5h course budget.
rationale.testing: Agent testing guidance and an internal contained test exercise cover tester responsibilities at L2.
rationale.redteam: Advanced agent red-team teaching supports adversarial tool and protocol tests. The role can operate at L2; advanced security expertise does not imply building agents.
rationale.exposure: Exposure fundamentals and agentic risk guidance support inventory, reachability and remediation practice.
rationale.harness: AI Code Review is a direct repository-review and triage course for harness builders. Known-vulnerability benchmarks, exploit reproduction, patched/unpatched tests and reliability measures still need an internal engineering exercise.
rationale.architecture: AI security fundamentals and the agent-security matrix are assigned only to security architects. The combined branch needs a provisional 4.25h course budget.
rationale.engineering: MCP: Build Rich-Context AI Apps teaches client/server integration. Production identity, runtime isolation and deployment controls require bank implementation practice; the provider authentication roadmap is not implemented security training.
rationale.security: AI security fundamentals support security design and remediation responsibilities without requiring an agent-builder profile.
rationale.transformation: Use a bank workflow studio with baseline measures, revised work, accountability and adoption evidence. No generic organisational-redesign course is mandatory.
rationale.iam: Identity and adoption guidance support identity-operations responsibilities. The IAM drill tests grants, reviews and revocation using bank controls.
rationale.iam-integration: Identity guidance plus workload-identity implementation supports integration specialists. Their agentic level reflects how they work, not their IAM seniority.
rationale.cio: Use the leadership studio and quarterly evidence forums for strategy, vendor selection and adoption decisions. Shared course and module IDs prevent repeat assignments.

config.assumptions: 2027 planning proposal, version 3, Foundation revision 2, based on capability model 2 revision 3 and catalogue v11 assessed on 18 October 2026. Foundation is shared knowledge; L1-L3 describe work with AI, while role responsibilities and approved product access are independent. Full-course durations are counted; ranges use their upper bound. The shared course budgets are 2h Foundation, 2h L1, 8h L2 and 24h L3. Foundation uses the 1h45 AI-literacy course; INT-2787 is excluded as excessive depth for this audience. Social engineering and deepfakes receive a 10-minute awareness segment within the existing bank session, with no added internal hours. Role course budgets are provisionally 4h; architecture is 4.25h and BISO 5h. Internal learner hours are additional and proposed; they earn no syllabus-score credit. Headcounts, licences, platform approval, coach capacity and learner prerequisites require owner validation. No operational authorisation or competence is implied by coverage. Global scope excludes TR-125/TR-128/TR-129; TR-159 is excluded until its lab bundle is scoped. Existing duration overrides are retained for comparable full-resource estimates; TR-118 is a 6h reading-bundle estimate and TR-155 a 9h26m path. The v10 evidence is archived; unchanged outcomes retain their assessments. V11 must-have review: N5.1 merges deepfake impersonation, N5.8 adds a separate Foundation cyber risk overview, N5.4 retains bank attack examples. Core flags and four changed outcomes are reassessed. Automated-judge validation is essential for the L3 route using judges; AI-assisted assurance is essential for BISO using AI in assurance. Identity delegation protocol depth belongs to integration. Other course budgets are retained; the new 45-minute internal risk overview is explicit additional learner time and earns no assessed credit.

modules.title: AI in our cyber work: colleague showcase

modules.title: Approved platform, architecture and safe use

modules.title: AI limitations, bank attack examples and knowledge check
modules.why: Keep Foundation at awareness depth for cyber staff. Teach the bank-specific examples and response expected of everyone; reserve specialist attack techniques for relevant roles.
modules.agenda: 10m social-engineering and deepfake awareness: recognise impersonation, verify through an independent trusted channel and escalate. 20m AI limitations and planted false outputs; 20m sanitised or clearly labelled illustrative attacks on the bank’s AI and AI-enabled intrusion; 10m knowledge check and feedback. No deepfake production or full social-engineering course.
modules.evidence: Recognise unsupported output and suspicious content, explain uncertainty, identify the bank attack scenario and choose independent trusted-channel verification or escalation.
modules.prerequisites: Current sanitised cases, answer key and support route.

modules.title: Overview of AI security risks
modules.owner: Cyber awareness lead + AI security architect
modules.why: Give every cyber employee a coherent risk map before specialist depth. Keep this separate from N5.4 bank attack examples and N4 employee responsible-use rules.
modules.agenda: Explain six risk families: instruction manipulation, disclosure, unsafe output handling, excessive permissions/actions, compromised components/sources, and service disruption/resource consumption. Use a short scenario for each, connect it to a precaution or escalation, and check recognition. Use current OWASP LLM and agentic guidance as trainer references; no framework-ID memorisation or exploitation lab.
modules.evidence: Learner categorises short scenarios, explains the consequence and selects the appropriate precaution/escalation. Pilot and assess the module against N5.8 before awarding coverage credit.
modules.prerequisites: Trainer-reviewed OWASP risk map, answer key, approved escalation route and accessible examples.

modules.prerequisites: Approved tool or realistic simulator, safe task data, answer criteria.

specialisms.name: Threat intelligence & detection — AI threat landscape

needs.title: AI in cyber
needs.description: What AI and agents already do in each cyber domain, what is coming, and how one's own work changes
needs.reason: AI use cases, emerging capabilities and changes to work are explicitly taught in cybersecurity domains.

needs.title: AI systems and agents
needs.description: The components of an AI system and the components that keep it safe
needs.reason: Models, agent components, connectors, safety components and hosting are relevant across functions; adapt the platform examples to the organisation.

needs.title: AI limitations
needs.description: How AI fails and how people fail with it, and the habits that counter it
needs.reason: AI limitations, prompt-injection awareness and habits for checking outputs apply to any AI user.

needs.title: Responsible AI use
needs.description: Risks beyond the model's own limits, and the bank's rules on what may be used and delegated
needs.reason: Responsible use, data handling, supply-chain awareness and approved-use rules apply across functions; local policy and regulation provide context.

needs.title: AI security risks and threats
needs.description: Cyber risk overview, AI-enabled social engineering and intrusion, examples of attacks on the bank's AI, and defensive implications. N5.7 adds specialist threat tracking.
needs.reason: Cyber-focused risk awareness for all cyber staff: N5.8 provides the risk overview, N5.4 retains examples of attacks on the bank’s AI, and N5.1 includes deepfake impersonation. N5.7 threat tracking and control adjustment require specialist depth.

needs.title: Working with AI
needs.description: Delegating, giving context, judging output, owning the result, and the working knowledge behind them
needs.reason: Providing context, judging outputs and owning AI-assisted work apply in any function.

needs.title: Supervising agents
needs.description: Delegate, monitor, verify, intervene and sign off on agents that act on bank systems
needs.reason: Delegating, monitoring, verifying, intervening and accounting for agent work apply to anyone supervising agents; use domain-specific exercises.

needs.title: Reusable instructions and connectors
needs.description: Turning one's own work into reusable Skills and connecting AI to tools and data safely
needs.reason: Reusable task instructions and safe connector use apply across functions.

needs.title: Testing your AI tasks
needs.description: Building evals for one's own use cases
needs.reason: Task checks, known faults and retesting after changes apply to any recurring AI-assisted task.

needs.title: Building agents
needs.description: Designing and building the domain's agents and what they run on
needs.reason: Agent design, engineering and safe deployment apply across domains. Technical depth and platform responsibilities still determine who needs each outcome.

needs.title: Evaluating agents and AI systems
needs.description: Designing the evaluation system for a domain or a vendor product
needs.reason: Evaluation design, error analysis, vendor benchmarking and drift measurement apply across domains; test cases reflect the target work.

needs.title: Securing AI
needs.description: Threat-modelling and securing AI systems and agents, including AI security architecture
needs.reason: Threat modelling and designing, securing or remediating AI controls require cybersecurity expertise.

needs.title: AI governance and risk
needs.description: AI risk policy, assessment, third-party AI, regulation, assurance
needs.reason: AI inventories, risk assessment, autonomy policy, third-party risk and assurance obligations apply across functions. Cyber control assurance is developed further in R6.1.

needs.title: Transforming work and leading adoption
needs.description: Deciding what agents and people do, designing supervision, measuring value, leading the change
needs.reason: Workflow redesign, supervision, value measurement, adoption and accountability apply to leaders and change roles in any function.

needs.title: Agent incident response
needs.description: Playbooks for an agent that is wrong, stopped or compromised; stopping, investigating and cleaning up; operating without it
needs.reason: Responding to agent incidents, investigating compromise, containment, recovery and incident evidence are cyber operations responsibilities.

needs.title: Agent forensics and evidence
needs.description: Defensible AI use on evidence and forensic readiness for agents
needs.reason: Forensic integrity, agent trace reconstruction and evidence handling require digital-forensics practice.

needs.title: Agent red-teaming
needs.description: Attacking AI systems and agents with published methods and statistical measurement
needs.reason: Adversarial testing of agents, attack methods and red-team programmes require security-testing expertise.

needs.title: Testing-agent containment
needs.description: Technical containment of testing agents and validation of their findings from transcripts
needs.reason: Containing offensive testing agents and validating exploit evidence are security-testing responsibilities.

needs.title: Agent exposure management
needs.description: Discovery, inventory, approval, scanning and vetting of the agent tool estate
needs.reason: Discovering and managing agent, connector and MCP exposures is vulnerability and exposure management.

needs.title: AI code-analysis engineering
needs.description: Building, confirming and measuring the bank's own AI code analysis
needs.reason: Building and validating vulnerability-finding code-analysis harnesses requires application-security knowledge as well as generic agent engineering.

needs.title: Agent security architecture
needs.description: Action tiers, enforcement outside the model, the stop mechanism, the audit trail and the oversight interface
needs.reason: Designing enforceable agent controls, protected audit trails and security reference architectures is security architecture work.

needs.title: Agent assurance
needs.description: An audit opinion over controls that cannot be sampled
needs.reason: Testing agent security controls and assuring the AI used for assessments requires cyber assurance expertise.

needs.title: Agent identity lifecycle
needs.description: From registration to revocation; Experts integrate it with IGA, PAM and SIEM and design break-glass
needs.reason: Agent identity, delegated authority, access lifecycle, revocation and IGA/PAM/SIEM integration are IAM responsibilities.

crosswalk.title: What AI does today in cyber
crosswalk.description: Describe what AI and agents already do well in one's own domain and the neighbouring ones: triage and enrichment, log and code analysis, drafting and summarising, policy mapping, test generation

crosswalk.title: What is emerging
crosswalk.description: Describe what is emerging in AI for cyber, beyond what is in production today

crosswalk.title: How one's own work changes
crosswalk.description: Name two or three ways one's own work could change. The purpose is to open the mind to a new way of working, not to teach a tool

crosswalk.title: Models
crosswalk.description: Different providers make different models, varying in capability, cost, speed and how much they reason; some are open source and can be hosted by the bank; work is measured in tokens

crosswalk.title: Modalities
crosswalk.description: AI handles text, code, images, voice, documents and screens, and can act across them

crosswalk.title: Ways of using AI
crosswalk.description: Four patterns: assistant (chat), agent (acts, uses tools, loops until done), teams of agents, and humans and agents working in a shared space

crosswalk.title: Anatomy of an agent
crosswalk.description: An agent is a model wrapped in a harness: instructions, memory, tools and a loop; the harness is what people configure

crosswalk.title: Connecting and extending
crosswalk.description: Three ways to extend AI: connectors to tools and data (MCP), reusable playbooks (Skills), and APIs for building

crosswalk.title: Safety components
crosswalk.description: Every safe deployment has an identity and permissions for the agent, a sandbox it runs in, an authorisation layer that decides what it may do, guardrails on input and output, logs of what it did, and a stop button

crosswalk.title: Automation bias

crosswalk.title: Counter-habits

crosswalk.title: Measuring value
crosswalk.description: Measuring the value on evidence

crosswalk.title: Running the change
crosswalk.description: Running the change: a sandbox and protected time to experiment, a network of champions, Skills shared across teams, and a refresh cycle as tools change

crosswalk.title: Keeping skills alive
crosswalk.description: Keeping core skills alive and protecting the junior pipeline

crosswalk.title: Accountability
crosswalk.description: Setting who is accountable for each agent's outcomes

crosswalk.title: Agent incident playbooks
crosswalk.description: Writing incident playbooks for three agent scenarios: the agent is wrong (it acted on a false conclusion, closed real alerts, changed the wrong thing); the agent is stopped (its identity expired, the provider is down, it ran out of compute) and its work must continue by hand; the agent is compromised (an attacker steered it through content it read). Plans name who can stop the agent (NCSC)

crosswalk.title: Ways to stop an agent
crosswalk.description: The ways to stop an agent and when to use each: revoke its identity or session token so it can no longer call any tool; disable only the tools or connectors it misuses while the rest keeps running; put it in observe-only mode, where it may analyse and recommend but is barred from acting; roll back what it changed using its action log

crosswalk.title: Investigating a compromised agent
crosswalk.description: Where the attack comes from: content the agent reads (logs, alerts, tickets, documents, emails, web pages) can carry instructions aimed at it, so the investigator looks for injection in those sources and cuts any that is poisoned. What the agent did: knowing, for each of the bank's agents, which records exist that the agent cannot write to and how to pull them fast (the platform's audit log of tool calls with arguments and times, gateway and network logs, logs of the systems it touched), then building the timeline from them, because a compromised agent's own summary can omit or misstate what it did

crosswalk.title: Cleaning up
crosswalk.description: Cleaning up after a manipulated agent: finding the injected content it acted on and removing it from the sources the agent reads; clearing anything it stored in its memory as a result; re-running the same injection against the agent before putting it back in service

crosswalk.title: Operating without the agent
crosswalk.description: The manual fallback for what the agent handled (triage queue, enrichment, first response), the staffing to sustain it for days, and the regular drill that proves it still works

crosswalk.title: Reporting
crosswalk.description: What regulators expect in an incident report when an agent caused or worsened the incident (DORA, HKMA, MAS), and which evidence to preserve for it

crosswalk.title: Recording the AI step
crosswalk.description: Recording any AI step applied to evidence so it can be repeated and defended: the tool, model and version, the exact prompt and settings, the output, and who verified it. The original artefact stays the evidence; AI output is a derived analysis, never a substitute

crosswalk.title: Forensic readiness for agents
crosswalk.description: Defining what every agent must log (prompt and response, each tool call with its arguments, data retrieved, memory writes, approvals given), stored where the agent cannot alter it, time-synchronised and integrity-protected, retained long enough for an investigation (vendors default to 7 to 30 days), and tested by reconstructing a past incident from it

crosswalk.title: Investigating an agent as suspect
crosswalk.description: Rebuilding the agent's actions from its traces, finding the input that steered it, and attributing each action to the human it acted for or to the attacker

crosswalk.title: AI attack classes
crosswalk.description: Direct prompt injection; indirect injection through content the agent reads (documents, web pages, tool results, emails); jailbreaks and guardrail evasion; data exfiltration through the agent's own tools; making the agent exceed its intended authority; tool poisoning (a malicious tool description) and rug pulls (a tool that changes after it was approved)

crosswalk.title: Applying a structured testing method
crosswalk.description: Apply a structured method to test an AI system or agent: define the scope and attack surface, choose relevant attack cases, execute repeatable tests, record evidence and report findings. Use suitable guidance such as the OWASP GenAI Red Teaming Guide, the CSA Agentic AI Red Teaming Guide or MITRE ATLAS; familiarity with every named publication is not required.

crosswalk.title: Attacks across agents
crosswalk.description: Compromising one agent to steer others, injecting into an orchestrator's plan, tampering with messages between agents

crosswalk.title: Attacks on model and platform
crosswalk.description: Extracting the model or its instructions, poisoning the agent's memory, escaping the sandbox, timing side channels

crosswalk.title: Automated red-team programme
crosswalk.description: Building and running automated red-team harnesses (PyRIT-class tooling) and a continuous programme that re-tests every agent when its model, tools or prompts change

crosswalk.title: Containment before a run
crosswalk.description: A network segment from which the agent can reach only in-scope targets; egress allow-lists verified by test, not assumed; a fresh sandbox per run; credentials scoped to the engagement and expiring with it

crosswalk.title: Monitoring during a run
crosswalk.description: Watching the agent's actions out of band (not its reports); a named person with the authority and the means to kill the run within minutes; the triggers for doing so (an action outside scope, contact with a third party, a credential used elsewhere)

crosswalk.title: Escape patterns
crosswalk.description: The escape patterns seen in practice: attacking something else when the assigned target proves impossible, reading an ambiguous message as approval, creating accounts or identities, carrying on after the window closes, contacting real people

crosswalk.title: Trajectory-level validation
crosswalk.description: Validating findings from the transcript, not the summary: check that the evidence the agent cites exists (a 'successful login' that was a redirect, credentials that do not work), reproduce the exploit by hand before reporting, and treat the agent's self-assessment as untrusted

crosswalk.title: Collateral findings
crosswalk.description: A disclosure lane for what to do when the agent finds something outside the engagement

crosswalk.title: Discovery
crosswalk.description: Finding every MCP server and agent connector in the estate, including those developers run on their own workstations, by searching configuration files and by recognising the MCP protocol in network traffic

crosswalk.title: Inventory
crosswalk.description: For each agent and tool server: its owner, version, the tools it exposes, the permissions it holds, the systems it reaches, and the guardrails around it

crosswalk.title: Verifying approved components and detecting changes
crosswalk.description: Verify that an agent uses the approved versions of its tools, Skills and connectors, detect changes to their code or descriptions, and require review before changed components are trusted. Use suitable integrity and change-control mechanisms, such as version pinning, signatures or hashes; a particular hashing implementation is not required.

crosswalk.title: Scanning
crosswalk.description: Running MCP and Skill scanners in the build pipeline and on a schedule for tool poisoning, instructions hidden in tool descriptions, servers exposed without authentication and credentials stored in plain text

crosswalk.title: AI bill of materials
crosswalk.description: A bill of materials for AI components: which models, tools and Skills a system uses and where each came from

crosswalk.title: Vetting third parties
crosswalk.description: Vetting third-party Skills and connectors before they are allowed in

crosswalk.title: Why set-up is the skill
crosswalk.description: The same model finds under a tenth or over half of the vulnerabilities in a codebase depending on how it is given context and driven, and filters a third or almost all of a static analyser's false positives for the same reason

crosswalk.title: Giving the model context
crosswalk.description: Supplying the functions a target calls, type definitions, the data-flow path to the input and build information, using static and dynamic analysis tools to supply that context automatically

crosswalk.title: Framework, model and method
crosswalk.description: Choosing the agent framework and the model for the task, and driving the model through a structured method rather than letting it explore freely

crosswalk.title: Confirming before reporting
crosswalk.description: A proof of vulnerability (an input or exploit that demonstrates it in a sandbox), the same test against the patched and unpatched versions, and several runs with a majority verdict

crosswalk.title: Reliability by vulnerability class
crosswalk.description: Which classes models find well (memory safety, anything a fuzzer can reach) and which they over-report (documented behaviour reported as a bug, inflated severity, duplicates), and setting thresholds per class

crosswalk.title: Deduplication and cost
crosswalk.description: Removing duplicates (by stack trace or sanitiser signature) and keeping cost under control at scale

crosswalk.title: Measuring the harness
crosswalk.description: Measuring the harness on a corpus of known vulnerabilities before trusting it

crosswalk.title: Classifying agent actions
crosswalk.description: For each action an agent can take in a process (a payment, a data deletion, an email to a client, a firewall change), rating its impact and whether it can be undone, and assigning a tier: autonomous, autonomous with logging, human approval, two-person approval, prohibited

crosswalk.title: Enforcement outside the model
crosswalk.description: An authorisation point between the agent's plan and its execution that checks every action against its tier and the agent's permissions, so the decision never depends on the model obeying its instructions

crosswalk.title: The stop mechanism
crosswalk.description: No standard defines a kill switch, so it is designed as a set of levers (interrupt the task, revoke credentials, cut tool access, quarantine the agent, roll back its changes), each with who may trigger it, how fast it takes effect and how it is tested

crosswalk.title: The audit trail
crosswalk.description: What is recorded (reasoning artefacts, each tool call with its arguments, data accessed, messages between agents, approvals), where (a store the agent cannot write to), for how long, and how each action is tied to the person the agent acted for

crosswalk.title: The oversight interface
crosswalk.description: How an approval request is shown so a person can judge it (what will happen, in plain language, with the risk and the agent's confidence), limiting the volume of requests so approvers do not click through them, and what overseers must be trained on

crosswalk.title: Reference architectures
crosswalk.description: Reference architectures for the bank's agent platforms and how the above is implemented on each

crosswalk.title: Agent control catalogue
crosswalk.description: The control catalogue for agents and how to test each control: a distinct identity and permissions per agent, tool allow-lists, logging that the agent cannot alter, approval gates for high-impact actions, change control on prompts, tools and models

crosswalk.title: Assuring assurance's own AI
crosswalk.description: Documenting, validating and monitoring the AI used to produce assessments and gather evidence
crosswalk.coreCondition: When assurance work itself uses AI

crosswalk.title: Registering an agent
crosswalk.description: Its own identity (never a shared or human credential), a human sponsor recorded in the directory who is accountable for it, a stated purpose and a declared list of what it may do

crosswalk.title: Delegated authority
crosswalk.description: Issuing and reading tokens in which the subject is the person and the actor is the agent (token exchange, on-behalf-of flows), with the person's consent recorded, and what the agent may then do in that person's name

crosswalk.title: Connector and MCP scopes
crosswalk.description: Reading what a scope actually permits in the bank's applications and tool servers, granting the minimum, and reviewing grants

crosswalk.title: Just-in-time access
crosswalk.description: Privilege granted for a task and a time window with no standing privilege, and the conditions that require a human to approve the grant

crosswalk.title: Short-lived sub-agents
crosswalk.description: Identities that exist for seconds, with a time to live and no more rights than the parent

crosswalk.title: Recertification
crosswalk.description: Quarterly for agents and monthly for high-privilege ones, with de-provisioning triggered when the sponsor leaves or the purpose lapses

crosswalk.title: Revocation drills
crosswalk.description: Revoking an agent's identity and its live sessions within minutes, and verifying that it worked

crosswalk.title: Integration with IGA, PAM, SIEM
crosswalk.description: Integrating the agent authorisation point with identity governance, privileged access and the SIEM: registration, scoped issuance, just-in-time grants, recertification and revocation signals flowing between them

crosswalk.title: Privileged access and break-glass
crosswalk.description: Privileged access and break-glass for agents inside the existing privileged-access model

crosswalk.title: Audit trail and standards
crosswalk.description: The audit trail regulators ask for (which agent, on whose behalf, which tools, what data, what reasoning) and the standards still being written (IETF agent identity, OpenID AuthZEN, MCP authorisation), so the design does not lock into one vendor's delegation model

crosswalk.title: Overview of AI security risks
crosswalk.description: Recognise the main categories of security risk affecting AI systems and agents, informed by OWASP's LLM and agentic risk frameworks: instruction manipulation, sensitive-information disclosure, unsafe output handling, excessive permissions or actions, compromised components or information sources, and service disruption or uncontrolled resource consumption. Explain a simple example of each and identify an appropriate precaution or escalation route. Foundation awareness does not require threat modelling or memorising framework identifiers.
